---
title: "The accounts data: mostly balance sheets"
---

## Summary

Almost every UK company must file annual accounts, and Companies House publishes the
electronically filed ones as a free bulk archive. But **what** a company files depends on its
size, and most UK companies are small or micro. Small and micro companies may file **"filleted"
accounts** — the balance sheet and its notes only, with no profit-and-loss account. The
practical result is that, for most companies, the public data has **no turnover and no profit
figure at all**: it is, in effect, a balance-sheet dataset. Accounts are tagged in **iXBRL**, a
format that is both human-readable in a browser and machine-readable, so the figures can be
extracted at scale.

Two changes matter for anyone using this data. Size thresholds rose on **6 April 2025** (their
first change since 2013), moving some companies into lighter-disclosure bands. And from **April
2028**, reforms will require small companies to file a profit-and-loss account — but that will
not fill in the past, so anyone modelling history still works with balance-sheet-only data.

## Details

### Who files what

Under the Companies Act 2006, essentially every registered company must file annual accounts
(private companies have nine months after the year-end). A company's **size band** is set by
meeting two of three tests — turnover, balance-sheet total, and average employees — over two
consecutive years. From **6 April 2025** the monetary thresholds rose by roughly half:

| Band | Turnover | Balance sheet | Employees |
|---|---|---|---|
| Micro-entity | ≤ £1m | ≤ £500k | ≤ 10 |
| Small | ≤ £15m | ≤ £7.5m | ≤ 50 |
| Medium | ≤ £54m | ≤ £27m | ≤ 250 |

Source: deck slides 11–12 and the accounts explainer
(`docs/source-material/accounts-explainer.html`); thresholds via Lexology summary of the
6 April 2025 change. **[Checked]** (official change date; figures are the published thresholds).

**Filleted accounts** are the defining feature. Under section 444 of the Act, small companies
and micro-entities prepare full accounts for their shareholders and HMRC, but file only the
**balance sheet and notes** with Companies House — omitting the profit-and-loss account and
directors' report. Since the overwhelming majority of UK companies are small or micro, the
public dataset is, in practice, a **balance-sheet dataset**.

> **What it means for you.** For most companies there is no turnover and no profit in the public
> data — not because the extraction missed it, but because it was never filed. One useful quirk:
> the *average-employees* note is generally treated as not a profit-and-loss note, so it usually
> survives filleting, which is why headcount is far better covered than any income-statement
> item. Credit agencies work around the missing turnover by **estimating** it from balance-sheet
> items and sector ratios (Creditsafe publicly describes an "Estimated Turnover Indicator") —
> these are modelled figures, not filed ones, so treat them with care.

### How it is tagged: iXBRL

**iXBRL** ("inline XBRL") is an ordinary-looking HTML accounts document in which each figure is
tagged with a machine-readable name. Concretely, a line that displays as "Equity 12,968" is
tagged in the HTML as something like:

```html
<ix:nonFraction name="Equity" unitRef="GBP" decimals="0">12,968</ix:nonFraction>
```

A browser renders "12,968"; a parser reads that the value 12,968 is `Equity`, in GBP. Each tag
also carries a reporting **period**, a **unit** (pounds, a count, a ratio), an optional
**scale** (for example, "thousands"), a **sign**, and optional **dimensions** (for example,
creditors split into "due within one year" and "after one year").

Tags follow **FRC taxonomies** — FRS 105 for micro-entities, FRS 102 (including Section 1A) for
small and larger companies — which define the machine-readable name for each figure. The
taxonomies are revised often, so this project targets each concept's stable *local* name and
reads across taxonomy generations without a version map. See [the accounts guide to
pitfalls](pitfalls.qmd) for what goes wrong at the tag level.

> **Why the data starts in 2014.** iXBRL adoption in the bulk product was gradual, not a hard
> cutover: roughly **0% of filings were iXBRL in 2010, rising through 2011–2013 and reaching
> ~97% by 2014**. Earlier accounts exist on the server but are barely machine-tagged, so the
> dataset starts in 2014 — a coverage decision, not a limit of Companies House's archive.
> Source: `docs/accounts-limitations.md` and deck slide 11 notes. **[Checked]** (project
> measurement).

### What's changing

| When | Change |
|---|---|
| 2008 | Bulk accounts product begins (e-filed only) |
| ~2014 | iXBRL nearly universal in the bulk data |
| 6 April 2025 | Size thresholds raised ~50% |
| 2025–26 | Identity checks for directors and PSCs (ECCTA) |
| April 2028 | Software-only iXBRL filing; small & micro firms must file a P&L |

The **2028 reforms** (Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023) will require small
companies and micro-entities to file a profit-and-loss account, move all filing to commercial
software in iXBRL, and remove the filleted/abridged options. After a pause, this was confirmed
on **9 June 2026 for April 2028** (delayed from 2027), and the government has indicated
small-company P&L data **may be kept private** rather than published. Source: ICAEW, June 2026
(deck slide 11 notes; accounts explainer). **[Checked]** as of June 2026 — the date has already
moved once, so re-confirm before relying on it.

> **What it means for you.** Future data will be richer, but **2028 does not fill in history**:
> past filings stay balance-sheet-only, and any newly required small-company P&L may stay
> private. Anyone modelling on the historical archive must work with balance-sheet-only data for
> the foreseeable future.
